content: Café au lait spots, also known as CAL spots, are pigmented birthmarks that appear on the skin. The term café au lait is derived from French, meaning coffee with milk, which describes their light-brown coloration in individuals with lighter skin tones. In individuals with darker skin, these spots may appear as darker lesions, sometimes referred to as café noir. From a pathophysiological perspective, café au lait spots are generally benign and not associated with medical complications in most cases. However, the presence of multiple café au lait spots (three or more) can be indicative of underlying genetic conditions, such as neurofibromatosis or the rare McCune-Albright syndrome. Specifically, the presence of six or more café au lait spots larger than 5 mm in diameter in prepubertal children, or larger than 15 mm in diameter in postpubertal individuals, is a key diagnostic criterion for Neurofibromatosis Type I (NF1). Café au lait spots can also be associated with other syndromes, including but not limited to: Fanconi anemia Tuberous sclerosis Russell-Silver syndrome (also known as Silver-Russell dwarfism) Ataxia telangiectasia Bloom syndrome Basal cell nevus syndrome Gaucher disease Chédiak-Higashi syndrome Hunter syndrome Maffucci syndrome Multiple mucosal neuroma syndrome, which is part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN2) Diagnosis of café au lait spots typically involves a thorough physical examination, with particular attention to the skin. The identification of café au lait spots, especially in conjunction with other clinical findings such as mental retardation (MR) in the case of McCune-Albright syndrome, can aid in diagnosing associated syndromes.
